summary: Defines OSPFv2 extensions for Bit Index Explicit Replication, an architecture for multicast forwarding that needs no per-flow state in intermediate routers and no explicit tree-building protocol. The extensions let routers advertise the information BIER needs.

plainLanguage.summary: BIER is a way of sending multicast traffic without the routers in the middle keeping per-flow state. Each packet carries a bit string, and each bit stands for one destination router. This document describes how OSPF routers tell each other which bit belongs to which router.

questions: how does ospfv2 advertise bier information
how does ospf advertise bier information
subtitle: How OSPFv2 routers tell each other the information BIER multicast forwarding needs, in MPLS networks.

tldr.problem: BIER forwards multicast packets by a bit in the packet header, so the routers in the path need to know which bit means which destination.
tldr.mechanism: Each BIER router advertises its own prefix with a BIER sub-TLV giving its identifier, its sub-domain and the MPLS label range it uses. OSPF floods these in Extended Prefix Opaque LSAs.
tldr.outcome: Every BIER router can build the forwarding table that maps each bit to a set of next hops. RFC 8444 is a Proposed Standard that was later updated by RFC 9272.

today: RFC 8444 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2018. It was later updated by RFC 9272, which added the constraints on underlay path calculation, and it has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: What BIER Changes
sections.content:
Bit Index Explicit Replication is an architecture that forwards multicast traffic optimally through a BIER domain without the intermediate routers keeping any multicast-related state per flow. It does not need a protocol that builds a forwarding tree either. A multicast data packet enters the domain at a Bit-Forwarding Ingress Router and leaves it at one or more Bit-Forwarding Egress Routers. The ingress router adds a BIER packet header, and that header holds a BitString in which each bit represents exactly one egress router to forward the packet to. The set of egress routers the packet must reach is expressed by the set of bits in that header.

BIER needs the routers taking part to exchange BIER-related information within a domain, and it allows a link-state routing protocol to distribute that information. This document describes the extensions to OSPF needed to advertise BIER-specific information when BIER uses MPLS encapsulation, as defined in RFC 8296. Other encapsulations, and the use of several at once, are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Ordinary multicast forwarding needs a tree, and the routers in it keep a record of every flow passing through. BIER replaces that with a bit string in the packet header: bit 3 means deliver to this router, bit 4 means that one. The routers only need to know which bit belongs to which router, so they keep no per-flow state and need no tree-building protocol.

sections.title: Where BIER Information Goes in OSPF
sections.content:
All the BIER-specific information a Bit-Forwarding Router needs to advertise to other such routers is associated with a BFR-prefix. A BFR-prefix is a unique routable IP address, unique within a given BIER domain, assigned to each BIER router as described in Section 2 of RFC 8279. Because the information has to hang off a BFR-prefix, the OSPFv2 Extended Prefix Opaque LSA of RFC 7684 is used to carry it.

Inside the Extended Prefix TLV there is a sub-TLV for distributing BIER information, called the BIER Sub-TLV, and several of them may be included in the same Extended Prefix TLV. The BIER Sub-TLV in turn may hold further sub-TLVs, one for each encapsulation the router uses.
sections.plainLanguage: Each BIER router has its own address in the routing protocol, and the BIER information is attached to that address. OSPF already has a way of attaching extra information to a prefix, and that is what is used here.

sections.title: The BIER Sub-TLV
sections.content:
The BIER Sub-TLV has Type 9 and a variable Length, because its size depends on the sub-TLVs it carries. Its fields are:

  • The sub-domain-id, a unique value identifying the BIER sub-domain within the BIER domain, as described in Section 1 of RFC 8279.
  • The MT-ID, the Multi-Topology ID of RFC 4915, identifying the topology associated with the BIER sub-domain.
  • The BFR-id, a 2-octet field encoding the identifier of the BIER router. If the router is not locally configured with a valid BFR-id, this field is set to 0, which RFC 8279 defines as illegal.
  • The BAR, a single octet giving the BIER Algorithm used to calculate the underlay paths that reach other BIER routers. The values come from the BIER Algorithm registry of RFC 8401.
  • The IPA, a single octet giving the IGP Algorithm used to modify, enhance or replace the calculation of those underlay paths, as defined by the BAR value. The values come from the IGP Algorithm Types registry.

Each BIER sub-domain MUST be associated with exactly one OSPF topology, identified by the MT-ID. If the association advertised by another router conflicts with the association configured locally on the receiving router, the BIER Sub-TLV for that conflicting sub-domain MUST be ignored, and the same is true if the MT-ID holds an invalid value. If a router advertises the same sub-domain-id in more than one BIER Sub-TLV, it MUST be treated as if it had advertised no BIER Sub-TLV for that sub-domain.

All BIER routers MUST detect the advertisement of duplicate valid BFR-ids for a given MT-ID and sub-domain-id, and when they do they MUST behave as described in Section 5 of RFC 8279.

The supported BAR and IPA algorithms MUST be the same on every router supporting a given BIER sub-domain. A router that receives a BIER Sub-TLV whose BAR or IPA field does not match its own local value for that sub-domain MUST report a misconfiguration and MUST ignore the sub-TLV containing the error. The use of non-zero values in either field is outside the scope of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: The sub-TLV names the sub-domain, the topology, the router's own identifier, and the two algorithms used to work out paths to the other routers. If two routers disagree about those algorithms, the receiver ignores the advertisement and reports a configuration error.

sections.title: The BIER MPLS Encapsulation Sub-TLV
sections.content:
The BIER MPLS Encapsulation Sub-TLV is a sub-TLV of the BIER Sub-TLV, and it carries the MPLS-specific information BIER needs. It MAY appear more than once in the BIER Sub-TLV. Its Type is 10 and its Length is 8 octets. Its fields are:

  • Max SI, a 1-octet field encoding the maximum Set Identifier used in the encapsulation for this BIER sub-domain and this BitString length.
  • Label, a 3-octet field whose 20 rightmost bits give the first label in the label range. The 4 leftmost bits MUST be ignored.
  • BS Len, a 4-bit field encoding the supported BitString length associated with this BFR-prefix. The allowed values are specified in Section 2 of RFC 8296.
  • Reserved, which SHOULD be set to 0 on transmission and MUST be ignored on reception.

The label range is the set of labels beginning with the Label and ending with Label plus Max SI. A unique label range is allocated for each BitString length and sub-domain-id, and these labels are used for BIER forwarding. The size of the range is set by the number of Set Identifiers used in the network, with each Set Identifier mapping to a single label: the first label is for SI 0, the second for SI 1, and so on.

If the label associated with the maximum Set Identifier exceeds the 20-bit range, the sub-TLV containing the error MUST be ignored. If the BitString length does not match any of the allowed values, the sub-TLV containing the error MUST be ignored. If the same BitString length appears in more than one of these sub-TLVs inside the same BIER Sub-TLV, the whole BIER Sub-TLV containing the conflict MUST be ignored. Label ranges within all the BIER MPLS Encapsulation Sub-TLVs advertised by the same router MUST NOT overlap, and if an overlap is detected all the BIER sub-TLVs advertised by that router MUST be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: This sub-TLV tells the other routers which MPLS labels carry the BIER traffic for each bit-string size. The labels run in a range, one per Set Identifier, and the ranges of different routers must not overlap.

sections.title: Propagating BIER Information Between Areas
sections.content:
The flooding scope of the OSPFv2 Extended Prefix Opaque LSA used to carry the BIER Sub-TLV is area-local. To allow BIER to be deployed in a multi-area network, OSPF has to propagate BIER information between areas.

When an OSPF Area Border Router advertises a Type-3 Summary LSA for an intra-area or inter-area prefix to all its attached areas, it also originates an OSPFv2 Extended Prefix Opaque LSA whose flooding scope is area-local and whose route type in the Extended Prefix TLV is inter-area. In deciding whether to include a BIER Sub-TLV in that LSA, the area border router examines its best path to the prefix in the source area and finds the advertising router associated with that best path. If that router advertised a BIER Sub-TLV for the prefix, the area border router copies the information from it when advertising to each attached area.

The example in the document has R1 advertising the prefix 192.0.2.1/32 in Area 1, along with an Extended Prefix Opaque LSA that includes a BIER Sub-TLV. The area border router R2 computes reachability for that prefix inside Area 1 and propagates it to Area 0, copying the entire BIER Sub-TLV it received from R1, with all of its sub-TLVs, into the Extended Prefix Opaque LSA it generates for 192.0.2.1/32 in Area 0. The area border router R3 then does the same from Area 0 into Area 2.
sections.plainLanguage: BIER information normally stops at the edge of an OSPF area. To carry it further, each area border router copies the BIER information it learned in one area into the advertisement it sends to the next area.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document introduces new sub-TLVs for the existing OSPFv2 Extended Prefix TLV and brings no new security risks to OSPF. The existing security extensions of RFC 2328 and RFC 7684 apply. It assumes that the BIER and OSPF layers are under a single administrative domain. Where potential attackers may have access to one or more networks in the OSPF routing domain, stronger authentication mechanisms such as those in RFC 7474 SHOULD be used.

The Security Considerations section of RFC 8279 discusses the possibility of a denial-of-service attack by setting too many bits in the BitString of a BIER-encapsulated packet. That attack cannot be started by modifying the OSPF BIER advertisements, because the ingress router decides which systems receive a BIER-encapsulated packet and that decision is not influenced by the OSPF control messages. The ingress router sets one bit for each destination system, and the OSPF advertisements are used only to build the forwarding tables that map each bit to a set of next hops, not to decide which bits to set. An attack on the OSPF control plane therefore cannot cause this kind of denial of service.

While a BIER-encapsulated packet traverses the network, a router that receives a packet with n bits set may have to replicate it and forward several copies. A given bit is set in only one copy, so each transmitted replica has fewer bits set, and so targets fewer destinations, than the packet that was received. This is an essential property of the BIER forwarding process. A failure of the process might cause a denial-of-service attack, but such a failure cannot be caused by an attack on the OSPF control plane.

Implementations MUST ensure that malformed BIER and BIER MPLS Encapsulation Sub-TLVs are detected and do not give an attacker a way to crash the OSPF router or routing process. Reception of malformed TLVs or sub-TLVs SHOULD be counted and logged for further analysis, and that logging SHOULD be rate-limited so that a denial-of-service attack cannot overload the OSPF control plane.
sections.plainLanguage: The new advertisements travel in the OSPF packets that already have their own security rules, so nothing new is needed. The one thing implementations must get right is rejecting malformed advertisements without crashing, and without logging so much that the logging itself becomes an attack.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA has allocated the following values from the OSPFv2 Extended Prefix TLV Sub-TLVs registry of RFC 7684: the BIER Sub-TLV is 9, and the BIER MPLS Encapsulation Sub-TLV is 10.
sections.plainLanguage: The document asks the registry for two numbers, 9 and 10, for the two new sub-TLVs.

viz.caption: THE FOUR PARTS OF BIER FORWARDING (RFC 8444, SECTION 1)

items.title: Bit-Forwarding Ingress Router
items.text: The router where a multicast packet enters the BIER domain. It adds the BIER packet header.

items.title: BitString
items.text: The bit string in the header, where each bit stands for exactly one Bit-Forwarding Egress Router.

items.title: Bit-Forwarding Egress Router
items.text: One or more of these receive the packet and take it out of the BIER domain.

items.title: No per-flow state
items.text: The routers in the middle keep no multicast-related state per flow, and BIER needs no protocol that builds a forwarding tree.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Variable, depending on the sub-TLVs carried inside.

fields.name: sub-domain-id
fields.desc: Identifies the BIER sub-domain within the BIER domain.

fields.name: MT-ID
fields.desc: The Multi-Topology ID of the topology associated with the sub-domain.

fields.name: BFR-id
fields.desc: The identifier of this BIER router. Zero means the router has no valid identifier configured.

fields.name: BAR
fields.desc: The BIER Algorithm used to calculate the underlay paths to other BIER routers.

fields.name: IPA
fields.desc: The IGP Algorithm used to modify, enhance or replace that path calculation.

viz.caption: THE BIER MPLS ENCAPSULATION SUB-TLV (RFC 8444, SECTION 2.2)

fields.desc: 10, the BIER MPLS Encapsulation Sub-TLV type.

fields.name: Max SI
fields.desc: The maximum Set Identifier used in the encapsulation for this sub-domain and BitString length.

fields.name: Label
fields.desc: A 3-octet field whose 20 rightmost bits give the first label of the label range. The 4 leftmost bits are ignored.

fields.name: BS Len
fields.desc: The supported BitString length associated with this BFR-prefix.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Should be set to 0 on transmission and ignored on reception.
